pg:https://www.wired.com/story/particle-.desc: An extremely rare matter-decay event opens up new possibilities for researching the physical world on scales 100 billion times smaller than an atom.
paras: While crashing protons together at nearly the speed of light, scientists at CERN found evidence of one of the most improbable decays of matter—so unlikely that it’s a phenomenon physicists have been hoping to observe for more than four decades. The collision produced numerous particles, including some known as neutral B mesons, and scientists found signals indicating that one of these had decayed into a muon and an antimuon.

Mesons decay all the time. These tiny particles, smaller than atoms, arise from collisions between other particles and exist only briefly before transforming into other particles. Muons, on the other hand, are similar to the electrons found in atoms, but about 200 times heavier. Scientists study these particles and their decays to test the predictions of current physics and search for clues to unknown particles.

The standard model—the sort of bible of particle physics—predicts that for every 10 billion decays of neutral B mesons, this transformation will occur once. In other words, even if scientists were to observe 10 billion of these particles decaying, they would expect to find, on average, only a single muon and antimuon. This discovery is the first time an experiment has obtained evidence of this phenomenon, the details of which the researchers have made available in a preprint on arXiv.

paras: Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter Telegram LinkedIn Whatsapp GENEVA: Three-quarters of the world’s displaced people live in countries severely exposed to climate-related hazards, the United Nations said on Friday, calling for urgent action to protect them. A report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), released days before the COP31 climate conference in Turkey, said nearly 90 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people faced severe risks linked to global warming.

People fleeing conflict, violence and persecution often end up in places struggling with severe drought, deadly floods and extreme heat, the agency said. Climate change is also threatening lasting solutions for the displaced: more than two-thirds of refugees who returned home in the first half of this year went back to countries highly vulnerable to climate hazards. In Syria, where nearly four million displaced people have recently returned, falling groundwater and climate shocks are threatening recovery, and flooding along the Euphrates in May damaged homes and displaced thousands again.

UNHCR warned that by 2050, one in three refugee settlements in sub-Saharan Africa could face 100 or more days of dangerous heat a year. Weather-related disasters have caused more than 255 million internal displacements worldwide over the past decade, or about 70,000 a day. This year’s exceptionally strong El Nino is expected to drive further displacement, with severe flooding forecast to displace up to three million people in Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan and Uganda by the end of 2026.

Michael Kuba (University of Naple Federico II, Italy), Tamar Gunit, Daniel Abed-Navandi (both from Haus des Meeres-Aqua Terra Zoo, Austria) and Xin offered young common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) tight holes to squeeze through and publish their discovery that common octopuses use different strategies depending on the size of the hole in Journal of Experimental Biology .

paras: It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills.

These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters.

As one of the few Brits deluded enough to spend six hours queueing at the Wii U’s midnight launch, I have a certain fondness for the game launch as a cultural event rather than just a weird display of performative consumerism. There was something heartwarming about seeing the video game hype cycle transformed into a shared experience.

paras: Unlike humans and other animals with rigid skeletons, octopuses have extremely flexible bodies built around what scientists call a muscular hydrostat, a system of muscles that provides both support and movement without bones.

Their eight dexterous arms can bend and elongate, while their central mantle can change shape. The animal's circulatory system is also suited to contortions: major blood vessels have muscular pumping systems that help keep blood moving locally even when part of the body is constricted.

The researchers made videos of three sub-adult common octopuses squeezing through an adjustable opening.
